revisions.title: The danger of equal measures
revisions.body: I read this opening as a warning about equal measures. Gratitude is imagined as something that can be multiplied, yet Socrates makes the conversation pause over whether mathematical equality can represent intellectual worth. The section therefore asks us to listen for a distinction between treating figures alike and judging them alike. That distinction gives the exchange its tension before any later argument begins.

I would hear Socrates’ reply as a playful refusal to let a numerical proportion settle a question of worth. The mathematical joke does more than decorate the exchange: it makes the listener feel how a tidy measure can flatten a meaningful difference. Stay with that resistance; it is the single pressure point of this opening.

revisions.title: A route for the search
revisions.body: The Stranger turns the search for the statesman into a sequence of divisions. First, he proposes a distinction between practical and purely cognitive sciences; then he divides the cognitive side between judging and commanding. The grouping of political, royal, household, and masterly roles clarifies the target’s family resemblance, but the statesman’s exact place in the final division is not yet settled.

Here the practical/cognitive division is proposed as the opening cut, not demonstrated as an exhaustive map of every science. The dialogue can use it as a working distinction while leaving its adequacy to later inquiry.

revisions.title: The cut reaches living herds
revisions.body: The Stranger’s method keeps narrowing without yet naming the final herd. He first places the kingly art among self-directing commands, then separates commands concerned with lifeless from living production. Within the living field, the statesman is likened to a herd-rearer rather than a keeper of one animal. One way to read the interruption is as disciplined postponement: the analogy has reached a herd, but has not yet specified which herd.

revisions.title: The cut must follow a kind
revisions.body: The Stranger turns a quick two-way proposal into a lesson about the cut itself. The human/beast division remains under examination, not yet secured, while the dialogue insists that a species and a part are not interchangeable. Read the correction as a demand for a sound division, not as a route toward a final human target.
If the practice may be called either herd-tending or communal care, what must the division itself prove before the inquiry proceeds?

revisions.title: Why the shepherd image fails as a definition
revisions.body: The initial division identifies political and kingly art as the knowledge of herding human beings. But the Stranger immediately tests that definition against rival crafts: merchants, farmers, millers, trainers, and doctors can all claim to care for humanity, even its rulers. The lesson is methodological: “human care” is too broad a mark. The statesman’s distinctive work must still be isolated.

revisions.title: The myth changes the scale
revisions.body: The myth changes the scale of the inquiry. A reported reversal in the stars becomes the Stranger’s cosmological thesis: the cosmos is sometimes guided by the god and, when released, turns back on its own course. Hear this as the myth’s governing frame—not yet as a demonstrated definition of the statesman.

At 268d, the Stranger is announcing a change of method, not teaching recognition. He proposes a fresh start by another road, mixing a kind of play with a great myth; afterward, he says, the inquiry will resume its earlier procedure of removing part from part. The myth is a tool of the investigation, not a paradigm case that lets us see the statesman in advance.

revisions.title: A category must survive division
revisions.body: Here the Stranger refuses to let a plausible classification count as a finished definition. Even granting an art for the biped herd, he says, does not warrant naming it kingship and statecraft at once; the next move is to divide human rule by compulsion and voluntariness. I read this as a methodological lesson: a category must not merely include its target; it must also distinguish that target from a contrary mode of rule.

revisions.title: The paradigm remains provisional
revisions.body: This stretch turns an unfinished account into a controlled example. The Stranger presents the paradigm method as a move from a smaller, familiar case toward the larger problem of the king, then applies it to weaving. The resulting identification of weaving with clothes-making is useful precisely as a first outline, not as the political art itself: the text soon marks the account as incomplete. Hear the example as a method for seeing, not yet as the answer.

At 279c–280a, the classificatory descent reaches a deliberately provisional stopping point. The Stranger names the art most concerned with clothes as clothes-making and says that weaving, insofar as it is the greatest part of making clothes, differs from it in name alone. That is the narrow claim secured here. The dialogue soon reopens the account, so the passage should not be heard as having already defined weaving’s subordinate preparations or its final operation.

revisions.title: Two measures, one practical test
revisions.body: One way to hear this passage is as a correction to two easy habits of judgment. “Greater” and “less” are first compared with one another; excess and deficiency are then considered against a mean—the fitting point for the matter at hand. The payoff, as I read it, is methodological: a discourse is not good because it is long or short, but because its divisions help the listener inquire more clearly. The mean is a test of fit, not an exact numerical standard.

revisions.title: The proposed test: knowledge, not a verdict
revisions.body: One way to read this unit is as a move away from visible labels of government toward a criterion internal to ruling: knowledge. The argument then makes that criterion difficult to claim. The Stranger presents kingly knowledge as unavailable to a multitude, while the draught-player comparison extends the scarcity argument rather than proving a precise headcount. The passage narrows the inquiry; it does not yet establish that a true ruler acts for the governed.

revisions.title: Law as an imperfect likeness
revisions.body: Here the Stranger makes knowledge—not wealth, consent, or the mere presence of laws—the test of correct rule: the right constitution is the one whose rulers truly know, whether they govern with laws or without them. The passage then turns to the law-as-copy problem: written prescriptions can stand in for expert judgment, but it would be absurd to forbid a returning expert to prescribe contrary to them. The tension is between fixed rules and judgment responsive to circumstances.

The Stranger gives the weaving a two-level order: first, the soul’s eternal element is joined by a divine bond; then its animal element is joined by human bonds. He defines the divine bond as a steadfastly true opinion about the beautiful, just, and good—and their opposites—arising in the soul. One way to hear the sequence is as a warning against treating cohesion as mere arrangement: the human work is presented as answerable to a prior moral orientation.
